Carotid artery stenosis

Two mouse studies report possible changes in cerebral perfusion and cognitive measures after PBM in models of carotid narrowing and chronic hypoperfusion. They do not test treatment of carotid plaque or stroke prevention in people.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

The 2019 journal paper found higher FDG-PET SUVr in near-infrared and white-light groups than in stenosis-only controls, while a 2026 mouse study reported higher regional flow and cognitive-test performance. Both publications are preclinical and provide no patient effect estimate.

Summary of the Evidence

Two mouse publications report favorable perfusion measures and some cognitive or tissue findings after near-infrared light treatment in carotid-narrowing models. The 2019 journal paper found higher FDG-PET SUVr in both near-infrared and white-light groups than in stenosis-only controls; the authors interpreted this indirect measure as recovered cerebral blood flow. A later study reported higher regional flow and better cognitive-test performance, with less neuronal loss but residual necrotic foci. Certainty for clinical perfusion or cognitive outcomes is very low (Lee et al. 2019; Kim et al. 2026).

Human and clinical evidence

No study has tested PBM in people with carotid artery stenosis. The experiments examine brain responses to experimentally induced hypoperfusion, not carotid plaque, stroke incidence, or other patient outcomes.

Animal evidence

The 2019 journal study induced bilateral common-carotid stenosis in mice and compared near-infrared treatment with white-light, stenosis-only, and normal groups, with about four to five mice per group. It applied 810-nm LED light over the head for 30 minutes, three times weekly for one month. FDG-PET SUVr was higher in both the near-infrared and white-light groups than in stenosis-only controls; the authors interpreted these indirect PET findings as cerebral blood flow recovering toward normal (Lee et al. 2019).

A separate 2019 SPIE conference abstract from the research group describes a similar mouse model, schedule, and PET assessment, but reports 20 mW total power rather than the irradiance described in the journal article. The reports may cover overlapping work, so the abstract is not treated as independent replication (Lee et al. 2019 SPIE abstract).

A 2026 journal study used a mouse model of chronic cerebral hypoperfusion and reported higher regional blood flow, especially in cortical and hippocampal regions, and better cognitive-test performance. Histology showed less neuronal loss and smaller perivascular spaces, although necrotic foci remained. Changes in BCL2 and HIF-1 were also reported (Kim et al. 2026).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 2019 journal study used transcranial 810-nm LED exposure at 300–600 mW/cm² for 30 minutes, three times weekly over one month. Its related conference abstract described a similar schedule but reported 20 mW total power, so the dose descriptions should not be combined. The accessible 2026 abstract does not report enough dosimetry to compare its intervention. Light delivered through a mouse skull does not establish how much reaches human brain tissue (Lee et al. 2019; Kim et al. 2026).

Interpretation

The mouse publications report encouraging perfusion, behavioral, and histology findings in induced chronic hypoperfusion. They do not demonstrate plaque regression or stroke prevention in people. The 2019 conference abstract may overlap with the journal experiment, and its FDG-PET/SUVr interpretation is indirect. The evidence remains preclinical.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for cerebral blood-flow or cognitive outcomes in carotid stenosis. Both publications are small mouse studies, and no patient study is available (Lee et al. 2019; Kim et al. 2026).

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Evidence is limited to two small mouse publications from related Korean research settings. The 2019 paper uses FDG-PET SUVr rather than a direct perfusion measure, and SUVr was higher in the white-light group as well as the near-infrared group compared with stenosis-only controls. Its related conference abstract may overlap with that experiment. The 2026 report adds regional-flow and cognitive findings but remains an animal model. No patient study supports clinical inference (Lee et al. 2019; Kim et al. 2026; Lee et al. 2019 SPIE abstract).
